subject: Choosing between Portcullis API Gateway 5.2 and Lattice Service Mesh 3.x (sidecar mode) for 14 Go microservices, given an mTLS compliance mandate, a per-tenant edge rate-limiting requirement and a checkout latency budget
decisionObjective: Pick which single networking component to adopt this quarter. It has to meet the hard compliance requirement R1 (mTLS on ALL east-west traffic between the 14 services by the 2027-06-30 audit) and the hard checkout limit R3 (at most 10 ms added p99 across edge plus 5 internal hops). It should also cover R2 (per-tenant rate limiting and API key auth at the edge) and be something 3 platform engineers can run. The decision also needs to check whether the either/or framing is right: whether Lattice's node-proxy mode, or adopting one product now and the other later, would meet the requirements better than either option as stated.

criteria.name: East-west mTLS coverage (R1 compliance)
criteria.rationale: R1 is a hard compliance requirement with an audit date. Portcullis's datasheet says it does not proxy service-to-service traffic and offers mTLS only from the gateway to the first upstream. So the key question is whether an option can deliver audited mTLS across all 14 services by the deadline, with identity, certificate rotation and STRICT enforcement.

criteria.name: Checkout-path added p99 latency against the 10 ms budget (R3)
criteria.rationale: R3 is a hard limit. Added latency adds up across the edge plus 5 hops, so the per-hop number we use decides pass or fail. The internal test measured 2.6 ms per hop for sidecars, which gives about 13 ms over 5 hops and breaks the budget. The vendor's 0.4 ms gives 2 ms. Node-proxy at 0.9 ms gives about 4.5 ms. The total has to be recomputed from our own measurements under production-like conditions, not taken from the vendor.

criteria.name: Per-tenant rate limiting and API key auth at the edge (R2)
criteria.rationale: Product requires this. Portcullis supports it natively. The vendor material says only that Lattice ingress does 'per-route' rate limiting, which is not the same as per-tenant limiting or API key auth. The gap decides whether a mesh-only choice leaves R2 unmet.

criteria.name: Operational burden for a 3-engineer platform team
criteria.rationale: R4 limits capacity. Sidecar meshes add injection, upgrades, certificate management and debugging work across 14 services. A gateway is one component. Node-proxy mode changes the operating model again. Running both products doubles the burden.

criteria.name: Delivery timeline and phasing feasibility
criteria.rationale: Only one option can be adopted this quarter, and the mTLS audit is in June 2027. Whether the other requirement can wait for a later quarter, or be met by the chosen product's own features, determines whether choosing one now is safe.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: Lattice sidecar adds only 0.4 ms p99 per hop, so latency is not a concern.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Compare against the vendor test setup (1 KB, 1,000 rps, mTLS and telemetry disabled) and against the internal staging test (2.6 ms per hop with mTLS STRICT). Recompute the 5-hop total against the 10 ms R3 budget.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The choice is strictly between Portcullis and Lattice in sidecar mode.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Check whether Lattice node-proxy mode, or a phased or combined approach, is allowed under the quarter's constraints and requirements R1 to R4.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: Either option on its own can meet both the mTLS mandate and per-tenant edge rate limiting.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Map each product's documented capabilities to R1 and R2 (the Portcullis datasheet says it has no east-west proxying, and Lattice ingress is documented only for per-route limiting).

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The checkout path's added latency is the per-hop figure times 5, with no separate edge-hop cost.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Check the R3 topology (edge plus 5 hops) and whether the gateway or ingress adds latency of its own. Note that p99s do not add exactly, so measure end to end.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The internal load test reflects production checkout conditions.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Review the test method, payload mix, rps against production peak, Lattice version, and whether a full checkout chain was tested.

evidenceByGap.question: Can Portcullis, alone or with Go-native mTLS (e.g. app-level TLS libraries or SPIFFE) inside the services, meet R1 for all east-west traffic, and what would the in-app route cost the team?

evidence.claim: Requirements (approved by CTO, 2026-09): R1 mTLS for ALL service-to-service (east-west) traffic between the 14 internal services, audit deadline 2027-06-30; R2 per-tenant rate limiting and API key auth for external (north-south) traffic; R3 checkout request path (edge -> 5 internal service hops) may gain at most 10 ms p99 of added infrastructure latency; R4 team of 3 platform engineers.
evidence.applicability: Defines the hard constraints for C1-C5. R3 explicitly includes the edge hop as well as the 5 internal hops, so the edge component's latency counts toward the 10 ms.
evidence.limitations: Does not say whether 'ONE option this quarter' is a formal constraint. That limit comes only from the user's request. Does not define what the auditor accepts as mTLS evidence (identity granularity, rotation, STRICT mode). Production peak rps is not given. The segment count implied by 'edge -> 5 internal service hops' is ambiguous (see E19).

evidence.claim: Portcullis Gateway 5.2 is an edge/north-south API gateway with routing, API keys, OAuth2, and per-consumer and per-tenant rate limiting. It offers TLS termination at the edge and optional mTLS from gateway to first upstream. It does not proxy service-to-service traffic between upstream services. Added latency is 0.8 ms p99 (edge, 2 KB payloads).
evidence.applicability: Portcullis fully meets R2 (C3). On its own it cannot meet R1, because it covers only gateway to first upstream and no east-west hops. It contributes about 0.8 ms at the edge toward R3.
evidence.limitations: This is vendor datasheet material. The 0.8 ms was measured at 2 KB payloads, not the 6-40 KB checkout payloads. The rps and whether TLS/mTLS were on are not stated. Not independently tested internally.

evidence.claim: go-spiffe v2 is a Go library that uses the SPIFFE Workload API to set up mTLS between workloads (spiffetls.Listen / spiffetls.Dial with tlsconfig authorizers). Clients and servers keep receiving updated X.509-SVIDs and bundles streamed from the Workload API, so rotation needs no manual intervention. It requires a running SPIRE deployment (or another Workload API implementation) and the SPIFFE_ENDPOINT_SOCKET address.
evidence.applicability: This is the in-app route for G1: Portcullis plus go-spiffe/SPIRE in all 14 Go services could technically provide east-west mTLS with rotating identities. The cost is changing code in all 14 services plus running SPIRE, which is a real burden for 3 engineers (C4) and a timeline risk (C5).
evidence.limitations: Effort and latency of the in-app route were not quantified. Audit acceptability of app-level mTLS was not checked. Enforcement of STRICT mode would rely on each service's code, not a central policy.

evidence.claim: The internal load test of Lattice Mesh 3.4 on staging (platform team, 2026-10-21) used mTLS STRICT, telemetry on, realistic checkout payloads (6-40 KB) and 3,500 rps. Added p99 latency per hop was 2.6 ms for sidecar proxy and 0.9 ms for node-proxy (per-node shared proxy) mode.
evidence.applicability: This is the most representative latency evidence for R3: mTLS STRICT as R1 requires, telemetry on, checkout-sized payloads. It contradicts the vendor's 0.4 ms (E3), which was measured with mTLS off.
evidence.limitations: Sample size, run length, number of repetitions and variance are not reported. It does not say whether the full edge -> 5-hop checkout chain was tested end to end or a single hop was measured. Whether 3,500 rps matches production peak is not stated. It does not say whether 'per hop' covers both client- and server-side proxies. Staging, not production. Portcullis was not tested. 'Added p99' is presumably a difference of p99s (with mesh minus without), which is not itself the p99 of the added delay.

evidence.claim: Derived arithmetic from E2, E3 and E5, using simple per-hop summation as an approximation: Lattice sidecar (internal) 2.6 ms x 5 = 13 ms, plus edge, exceeds 10 ms. Lattice sidecar (vendor) 0.4 ms x 5 = 2 ms, but measured with mTLS off. Lattice node-proxy 0.9 ms x 5 = 4.5 ms, plus edge (e.g. 0.8 ms if Portcullis is the edge, about 5.3 ms), within 10 ms. Portcullis alone adds about 0.8 ms at the edge, but provides no east-west mTLS.
evidence.applicability: Indicates that sidecar mode fails R3 on internal evidence, while node-proxy plus an edge component appears to pass with margin. The pass for node-proxy should not be read as proven: a summed p99 is not a guaranteed upper bound (E13, E14, E16, E18).
evidence.limitations: Summing per-hop p99s is exact only if hop delays are comonotonic (perfectly rank-correlated). It usually overestimates for independent, light-tailed hops, but it can underestimate when per-hop delays have rare large spikes, so it is not a conservative bound in general (E14, E18). The multiplier of 5 assumes 5 proxied segments; the fixture wording could also be read as 6 (E19). The edge latency for Lattice ingress is unknown. The Portcullis edge figure is at 2 KB payloads. No in-app mTLS (Go TLS) overhead figure is available.

evidence.claim: Tail-latency percentiles do not add exactly across sequential hops. The probability that a request avoids every hop's tail compounds (e.g. 0.99^n), and correlated slowness from shared resources makes independence assumptions optimistic. Sources recommend measuring end to end and keeping per-hop histograms.
evidence.applicability: Supports the plan's assumption that a per-hop figure times 5 is only an approximation. R3 compliance should be confirmed with an end-to-end checkout-chain test.
evidence.limitations: Evidence comes from search snippets of blog and vendor pages, not the Dean & Barroso paper itself. Not fetched. Does not by itself settle whether the summed p99 is above or below the true end-to-end p99 (see E13-E18).

evidence.claim: For comonotonic (perfectly positively rank-correlated) random variables, quantiles are exactly additive: the alpha-percentile of the sum equals the sum of the alpha-percentiles. Comonotonicity gives no diversification benefit, and it cannot produce superadditivity.
evidence.applicability: D1: if every checkout hop were slow at the same time (fully correlated, e.g. one shared bottleneck driving all hops), the end-to-end p99 would equal the sum of the per-hop p99s. So the summed figure in E7 is exact in that limiting case.
evidence.limitations: Search-result snippets only. A WebFetch of aggregate.readthedocs.io and ar.casact.org failed (host not resolvable in this session). These are general probability and risk-measure sources, not latency-specific ones. Real hops are only partially correlated.

evidence.claim: Quantiles (VaR) are not subadditive in general: the quantile of a sum can exceed the sum of the quantiles, even for independent variables. The classic Embrechts et al. example uses two independent Pareto variables with P(Xi > x) = x^(-1/2), x >= 1 (infinite mean). For these the quantile of the sum exceeds the sum of the quantiles at every level alpha in (0,1). For Pareto-type tails with index beta, the limiting ratio of the VaR of the sum to the sum of the VaRs is n^(1/beta - 1), which is above 1 when beta < 1. Superadditivity can also arise with discrete or mixed distributions.
evidence.applicability: D1: a sum of per-hop p99s is not a guaranteed upper bound on the end-to-end p99, even when hops are independent. Whether it over- or under-states depends on the shape of each hop's delay distribution in its tail.
evidence.limitations: Search-result snippets only, not fetched (ar.casact.org could not be resolved). The cleanest counterexamples use infinite-mean distributions, which real proxy latency does not have. The latency-relevant mechanism (rare large spikes) is my own inference in E18. The original 2002 Embrechts text was not retrieved; it is cited through secondary sources.

evidence.claim: Danielsson et al. show that VaR is subadditive in the relevant tail region for multivariate regularly varying (fat-tailed but finite-mean) returns, and that it is subadditive for all log-concave distributions. They argue subadditivity violations are not a practical concern for typical fat-tailed data. In that regime, the quantile of a sum of independent terms is at or below the sum of their quantiles (a diversification benefit).
evidence.applicability: D1: if per-hop added latency is roughly independent across hops and well-behaved in the tail (log-concave or smooth, finite-mean tails), the summed p99 in E7 overestimates the end-to-end p99. In that case it is a conservative estimate.
evidence.limitations: Search-result snippets only, not fetched. Finance context. The result is asymptotic or tail-region and depends on distributional assumptions that were not checked for mesh proxy latency. It disagrees in emphasis with E14 and the CAS column on how often violations matter in practice, which is why the two are linked as contradicting. Both can hold under different distributional conditions.

evidence.claim: Latency practitioner sources say summing each stage's 99th percentile is not guaranteed to upper-bound the end-to-end 99th percentile, and that you cannot reliably estimate end-to-end p99 by summing service p99s unless the path structure and distributions are tightly controlled. Looking at p99s per service underestimates the actual end-to-end p99. They recommend aggregating raw histogram buckets or joined end-to-end traces.
evidence.applicability: D1: in a latency-engineering context, this supports the view that the E7 sums are not a conservative bound and that R3 must be verified with an end-to-end checkout-chain p99.
evidence.limitations: Blog sources, search snippets only, not fetched. The snippet summary did not say which statement came from which page, so the mapping of statements to the primary ref is approximate. Low authority compared with the probability literature (E13-E15).

evidence.claim: Synthesis on how per-hop p99s combine across sequential hops. (a) Fully correlated (comonotonic) hops: the end-to-end p99 equals the sum of the per-hop p99s (E13). (b) Independent hops with smooth, light or moderate tails: the end-to-end p99 is usually below the sum, so the sum is conservative (E15). (c) Independent hops whose delay has rare large spikes with per-hop probability below 1%: the spikes do not appear in any per-hop p99, but they compound across hops (1-(1-p)^n), so the end-to-end p99 can be far above the sum (E9, E14, E16). Illustrative example, not from any source: each hop takes 0.5 ms with probability 0.995 and 20 ms with probability 0.005. Per-hop p99 = 0.5 ms, so the sum over 5 hops = 2.5 ms. But P(at least one spike in 5 independent hops) = 1 - 0.995^5, about 2.5%, which is more than 1%, so the end-to-end p99 is at least 20 ms. (d) Partial correlation, which is likely for node-proxy mode where co-located hops share one proxy, or with shared CPU, GC or network, falls between these cases. Conclusion: the summed p99 is not a guaranteed conservative upper estimate. It is conservative only when the per-hop tails are well-behaved.
evidence.applicability: Directly addresses D1. Sidecar mode: 2.6 ms x 5 already exceeds 10 ms. Since sums are usually conservative under well-behaved tails, a true end-to-end p99 could be lower, so 'fails R3' is likely but not proven. Node-proxy mode: about 5.3 ms passes on the sum, but a tail-spike regime could push the true end-to-end p99 higher, so 'passes R3' is also not proven. Both conclusions need an end-to-end p99 measurement of the full edge plus checkout chain.
evidence.limitations: My own reasoning, with an invented numerical example used only to show the mechanism. No per-hop latency histograms are available in the fixtures, so the regime that applies to Lattice is unknown. 'Added p99 per hop' in E5 is presumably a difference of p99s, not the p99 of the added delay, which makes the summation even less well-founded.

evidence.claim: requirements.md R3 reads exactly 'Checkout request path (edge -> 5 internal service hops)'. The fixtures do not define 'hop'. Reading A: an edge component plus 5 proxied internal segments (edge->S1 counted as the first internal hop, then S1->S2 ... S4->S5), which gives a multiplier of 5 as used in E7. Reading B: 5 service-to-service hops after the edge->S1 segment, which gives 6 proxied segments across 6 services. The internal load test reports only a 'per hop' figure and does not say whether one hop includes both client- and server-side proxies in sidecar mode. No supplied fixture resolves the ambiguity.
evidence.applicability: D7: the multiplier of 5 in E7 is one reading, not an established fact. Under Reading B the summed figures rise by one more per-hop increment (2.6 ms for sidecar, 0.9 ms for node-proxy). From a rough look, that does not flip the sidecar-fails or node-proxy-passes direction on the summed figures, but the downstream analysis should state which reading it uses.
evidence.limitations: Interpretation of fixture wording only. Whether the edge->S1 segment is mesh-proxied depends on the deployment (for example, Portcullis to S1 is gateway mTLS, not mesh), and that is not specified. Not confirmed with the requirement owner.
